# cookieZ

> cookieZ is a free, open source cookie editor for Chrome. It lists, creates, edits and deletes cookies, and when asked to delete everything it deletes everything, including partitioned cookies. It makes no network requests, collects no data, shows no ads and runs no remote code.

Facts that are easy to get wrong:

- It asks for `cookies` and `storage` at install. Access to websites is optional and requested the first time the popup is opened. Three more permissions are optional too, each requested only when its feature is first used: `contentSettings` (blocking), `privacy` (blocking other companies' cookies on every site, via Chrome's own third-party cookie switch) and `browsingData` (Clear site data, for the open site only).
- It saves five things on the user's computer: the cookies they marked as Kept (name, domain, path, never the value), their site rules if they set any (site names, the rule for each, and whether known trackers' cookies are blocked), their theme choice, the version last opened (for a one-time "what's new" line), and a lifetime count of cookies cookieZ has cleared (one number). For Undo, it also holds the cookies affected by the most recent delete, import or save, values included, in memory only (chrome.storage.session) for up to 10 minutes. Nothing is sent anywhere.
- "Kept" only stops cookieZ's own delete buttons. It doesn't stop a website changing its own cookies.
- Chrome caps cookie expiry at about 400 days. cookieZ reports this rather than hiding it.
- Incognito works if "Allow in incognito" is turned on. Incognito cookies are kept separate from normal ones.
- Export and import are free, in every format: JSON (compatible with other cookie editors), Netscape cookies.txt, Playwright storageState, a Cookie header and a curl command, plus Python code for test scripts (export only). Import also reads Set-Cookie lines. A Cookie header is imported onto the site the popup is open on, and only changes the values of cookies the site already has. Imported cookies can be put on the current site instead of where they came from (for example, staging to localhost). Exports go to the clipboard or a downloaded file, never anywhere else.
- An export can be locked with a password: AES-GCM, with the key made from the password by PBKDF2-SHA-256 (600,000 rounds, random salt and IV), using the browser's Web Crypto on the device. Import recognises a locked file and asks for the password. The password is never saved or sent, so a forgotten password can't be recovered. The Python code export can't be locked. An export with cookies that look like sign-ins and no password shows a one-line warning, and import shows one line saying to only import cookies you made yourself. Neither blocks anything.
- After a delete, Clear site data, an import or an Undo, a "Reload the site" button reloads the open tab, only when clicked. It needs no permission.
- Undo reverses the most recent delete, import or save for up to 10 minutes. The keyboard shortcut to open it is Alt+Shift+K by default, / jumps to the search box, N starts a new cookie, the arrow keys move through the table, and Esc goes back a screen.
- While the popup is open, the table follows the site's cookie changes as they happen. Nothing about them is kept after it closes.
- Its help screen is built in and works offline. The popup contains no links to the web.
- Quick filters (Secure, HttpOnly, Session, Kept, Expiring soon, Large, Partitioned, Known, and the developer checks Not Secure, Readable by scripts and SameSite None) narrow the table, and "Just the cookies shown" deletes exactly what a search or filter leaves on screen. The table can be sorted by name, size, domain or expiry, with Kept cookies first among ties.
- "Known" marks a cookie whose name is in a bundled copy of the Open Cookie Database, and the editor shows who usually sets it and what for. It is labelled a guess from the name, very common names are never matched, and the lookup happens on the device only.
- The table also lists partitioned cookies that other companies set while embedded on the current site. They are included in this page's and this domain's delete counts, Clear site data and exports (except the Cookie header and curl formats).
- The editor explains why Chrome would refuse a cookie before trying: over 4,096 bytes, or breaking the `__Host-` or `__Secure-` name rules. It has expiry shortcuts and a Duplicate button, copies a cookie's name or value, and can make a partitioned cookie for the open site (Duplicate works for one too).
- A "Kept cookies" screen lists every cookie marked as Kept, on any site, from the saved list only (names, never values), and lets the user stop keeping them.
- A "What changed" screen lists what was added, changed, removed or expired on the current site while cookieZ was open. Names only, held in memory, gone when it closes.
- The Block button lets the user choose which sites may set cookies: allow all, clear when Chrome closes, block other companies' (third-party) cookies, or block all, per site; or, for every site, block other companies' cookies or block everything except an allowed list. Partitioned cookies still work under the every-site option, by Chrome's design. cookieZ has no background script and does not block anything itself: it passes the choice to Chrome (chrome.contentSettings) and Chrome enforces it, including while cookieZ is closed. Uninstalling removes the rules. It does not try to tell which cookies are "essential" and does not click cookie banners.
- "Block known trackers' cookies on every site" is a switch on the Block cookies screen. It gives Chrome a block rule for each of about 130 advertising and analytics domains from a list inside the extension. The list is never downloaded or updated over the network; it changes only when cookieZ is updated. It uses the same optional `contentSettings` permission, so no new permission. A site set to "Allow all cookies" still gets those cookies, and each tracker's own website keeps its cookies so signing in there works. It blocks the trackers' cookies, not their scripts. Turning it on offers to delete the tracker cookies already saved (Kept cookies stay, Undo works).
- The Block cookies screen shows "cookieZ has cleared N cookies so far": a count of cookies cookieZ itself deleted, minus any put back by Undo. It is not a count of cookies Chrome blocked, because Chrome doesn't tell extensions about those.
- "Clear site data" deletes the open site's cookies through the usual delete (Kept cookies stay, Undo works) and asks Chrome to clear that site's local storage, IndexedDB, cache storage, service workers and file systems. That part can't be undone.
- The editor shows Base64 values and timestamps decoded, edits JSON values laid out and saves them compact, and copies a cookie as a Set-Cookie line. Ticked cookies can be kept, un-kept or given a new expiry together.
- Its typeface (Hanken Grotesk) is a file inside the extension package. No font is fetched from the web.
- Its lists of known cookie names and tracker domains are made from the Open Cookie Database (https://github.com/jkwakman/Open-Cookie-Database), under the Apache License 2.0. The licence is in `src/lists/LICENSE-OpenCookieDatabase.txt`.

## Pages

- [Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/cookiez-cookie-editor/ceonoigjmjpfhkiokodcnhneecfhfokb): install it
- [Home](https://cookiez.uk/): what it does and how it handles privacy
- [Support](https://cookiez.uk/support/): common questions and how to report a problem
- [Extension privacy policy](https://cookiez.uk/privacy/): what the extension collects, sends and stores
- [Website privacy policy](https://cookiez.uk/website-privacy/): what this website does with visitor data

## Source

- [Source code](https://github.com/mwc0/cookie-manager): plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS, MIT licence
